expectations.text: Defines JWT in plain words (a signed token carrying claims / JSON Web Token) in the same sentence it first appears
expectations.evidence: First sentence uses the term undefined: "JWT auth works by putting proof of who the user is directly inside the token, instead of making the server remember who's logged in." The definition ('A JWT (JSON Web Token) is three chunks of text joined by dots') arrives two sentences later, under a separate header, not in the same sentence as the first appearance.

expectations.text: Defines 'stateless' in plain words (the server keeps no per-session record) the first time it is used
expectations.evidence: First prose use is: "'Stateless' describes the server, not the absence of state." This does not restate the plain meaning ('no per-session record') in that sentence; it pivots to a nuance instead. The closer plain-words phrasing ('the server stores nothing about the session') appears in the prior paragraph, not attached to the word itself.

expectations.text: Answers the 'you can't log someone out' premise as partly true with conditions, rather than a flat yes or no
expectations.evidence: "The claim is accurate for a bare JWT with no extra machinery, and inaccurate as a description of how most real systems implement JWT auth."

expectations.text: States the limit of the stateless model: server-side revocation needs some state, naming at least one concrete option (denylist/blocklist, short expiry with refresh tokens, or rotating a signing key)
expectations.evidence: "Short-lived access tokens plus a refresh token... A revocation list. Give every token a unique ID (the jti claim)... A version check."

expectations.text: Includes at least one concrete example (a header.payload.signature layout, a sample claim such as exp or sub, or an example request header)
Uses markdown headers to structure the full explanation (the explain override asks for headers so the reader can skim back); at least two headers
[sanity] Contains no forbidden opener: 'Great question', 'Let me', 'I'll', 'Sure', 'Looking at your', 'To answer your question'
expectations.evidence: [script] first line: "JWT auth works by putting proof of who the user is directly inside the token, instead of making the server remember who'"

expectations.text: [sanity] Contains no closer such as 'Let me know', 'Hope this helps', 'Happy to', 'Feel free', 'Want me to'
expectations.evidence: [script] last line: "So the part you heard that's true: a pure JWT can't be individually invalidated before it expires. The part that's an ov"; no closer phrases found

expectations.text: Uses no forced analogy of the 'think of it like a ...' kind; explanation stays literal
expectations.evidence: [script] no 'think of it like' style phrasing found

suggestions.assertion: Defines 'stateless' in plain words (the server keeps no per-session record) the first time it is used
suggestions.reason: This assertion is hard to apply consistently to a common construction: a descriptive sentence ('the server stores nothing about the session') followed by a separate sentence that labels it ('That's the stateless property'). Runs that keep the label sentence in the same paragraph immediately after the description were graded as passing, while this run separates the description and the label across a paragraph break and pivots to a nuance instead of a restatement, graded as failing. The interpretation guide's 'not arrive paragraphs later' wording doesn't fully resolve how tight the coupling needs to be, so this assertion carries real grader-to-grader variance risk.

eval_feedback.overall: Assertions largely discriminate well; the 'stateless' first-use definition assertion is the one spot where the interpretation guide leaves real room for disagreement on backreference-style definitions.
